name: Positional Failures in Long-Context LLMs (arXiv:2605.23170)
publisher: Chuyifei Zhang, Hongyu Cui, Xiaowen Huang, Jitao Sang (institutional affiliations not stated on the arXiv listing page; likely a Chinese university lab given author names and venue pattern) [uncertain]
claim_value: Full title: 'Positional Failures in Long-Context LLMs: A Blind Spot in Reasoning Benchmarks.' The authors audit 11 long-context benchmarks and find none jointly controls task position, filler content, and context length for reasoning tasks (as opposed to pure retrieval tasks like Needle-in-a-Haystack/RULER, where position control is standard). An audit of four flagship long-context model releases finds no main result-table entry for NIAH, RULER, or LongBench-family benchmarks, while agentic/coding benchmarks appear in all four. They propose a new framework, Context Rot Evaluation (CRE), varying task position, filler content, and context length, and evaluate 9 LLMs on GSM8K and ARC-Challenge across two rounds (an initial 5-model set, then 4 newer vendor releases). Results: models can drop sharply in accuracy when the target task moves from the end to the middle of context, and this drop worsens with context length for vulnerable models. MiMo-v2-Flash drops 88 percentage points at 64K context under 'with_solutions' filler (middle-position accuracy falls to 8%). Newer model releases show smaller drops (3 of 4 stay within +/-6pp of end-position accuracy at 64K; MiMo-V2.5-Pro narrows the 88pp drop to 32pp), but under a different filler type ('questions_only_v2') middle-position drops persist across all four newer models (range -16pp to -56pp across 8K/32K/64K). A diagnostic probe (adding a copy of the target task at the end of an 8K context) brings middle-position accuracy within +/-4pp of the end-position baseline across all nine models, supporting a positional explanation. In the initial five-model set, 76% of middle-position errors matched surrounding filler text, versus 22% at end positions, consistent with filler-answer interference as the dominant failure mechanism (rather than pure attention/positional decay).
claim_definition: A benchmark/empirical result from an academic paper: it introduces a new controlled evaluation methodology (CRE) and reports accuracy deltas (in percentage points) across 9 LLMs, 2 reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, ARC-Challenge), 3 context lengths (8K/32K/64K), and multiple filler-content conditions, plus a benchmark-literature audit of 11 existing long-context benchmarks and 4 vendor model-card result tables.
reproducibility: The paper does not state in the extractable text whether code/data/the CRE harness is publicly released; no GitHub or repository link was found in the fetched abstract or PDF excerpts [uncertain]. As a May 2026 preprint, no independent third-party replication was found.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: No. The authors appear to be independent academic researchers; no vendor product, platform, or commercial context-engineering tool is promoted or sold by this source.
conflict_notes: No specific numeric discrepancy was found between this paper's findings and how it might be cited elsewhere, since it does not yet appear to be widely cited. One internal nuance worth flagging if cited elsewhere: the severity of the middle-position drop is highly filler-dependent and model-dependent (88pp for one older model under one filler type, but only 6pp or less for most newer models under the same filler type, while a different filler type still produces large drops on the same newer models) -- a secondary source could easily overstate or understate the effect by citing only the 88pp figure without the filler-type and model-version caveats.
relationship: Complicates the simple 'context engineering is what matters now' framing by showing that most reasoning benchmarks (as opposed to retrieval benchmarks) do not even measure positional sensitivity, meaning vendor claims of long-context robustness based on standard reasoning benchmarks may be systematically blind to a real failure mode. It supports the broader context-engineering thesis that *how* information is placed/structured in context materially affects output quality, independent of model choice or prompt wording, but it also shows the field's own evaluation tooling has a structural gap, which is itself a context-engineering-adjacent critique of benchmark practice rather than a simple confirmation of vendor narratives.
derivative_of: Explicitly extends 'Lost in the Middle' (Liu et al., 2023), which first showed LLMs struggle to access information placed in the middle of long contexts, and NoLiMa (Modarressi et al., 2025), cited as showing position bias affects reasoning benchmarks specifically. This paper's contribution is the CRE framework plus a systematic audit showing reasoning benchmarks (unlike retrieval benchmarks) generally fail to control for position, and a mechanistic finding (filler-answer interference) for why middle-position errors occur, which is a more specific causal mechanism than the attention-decay explanation often assumed from 'Lost in the Middle.'
register: Academic researcher audience primarily (an arXiv cs.CL paper introducing a new evaluation framework), with secondary relevance to enterprise IT buyers evaluating vendor long-context claims and practitioners designing benchmarks or context layouts for reasoning-heavy agents.

(2023) found that LLMs struggle to access information in the middle of long contexts'; 'Modarressi et al. (2025) introduced NoLiMa, showing that position bias affects reasoning benchmarks'). Author institutional affiliations could not be confirmed from the fetched content [uncertain]. Code/data availability could not be confirmed [uncertain].
new_angle: Adds a distinct mechanism and a methodological critique not previously logged: that mainstream reasoning benchmarks (unlike retrieval benchmarks) lack positional controls entirely, that vendors therefore cannot and do not report positional robustness for reasoning tasks, and that the dominant error mechanism at middle positions is filler-answer interference (wrong answers lifted from surrounding filler text) rather than pure attention decay. Provides a quantified, model-version comparison showing the failure mode is improving across newer releases for some filler types but persists for others, which nuances any blanket claim that 'lost in the middle' is a solved problem.
